summary: The AI buildout is more likely to resemble the 60-year railroad buildout than the telecom overbuild, if AI continues to become more economically useful
summary_extended: Baker argues that the current AI infrastructure buildout is structurally more analogous to the 60-year railroad expansion of the 19th century than to the late-1990s telecom overbuild, which collapsed catastrophically. His reasoning centers on token demand elasticity: as long as AI continues to become more economically useful and demand for inference and training compute grows with falling prices, capex will be sustained rather than reversed. He frames this as the central binary question he underwrites across his entire portfolio — railroad (sustained multi-decade buildout) versus telecom (overbuild and bust) — and explicitly states it is the primary question he asks management teams. The railroad analogy is quantified: the buildout lasted roughly 60 years at a GDP share comparable to current AI capex, implying the current cycle could have decades of runway if the demand elasticity condition holds. The investment implication is a long bias across AI infrastructure beneficiaries, contingent on continued evidence that AI is generating real economic value.
detail: Baker draws an explicit analogy: the railroad buildout lasted ~60 years at a roughly comparable percentage of GDP to current AI capex. If token demand elasticity remains positive and AI keeps getting more economically useful, the buildout continues rather than collapsing like telecom. This is the key binary he is underwriting.
